finalMessage: Teach the children. Shape the future. Save the Earth.
objective: Mars Academy aims to spark children's interest in science, technology and space exploration in a fun, interactive way, presenting the reality of Mars and the challenges of living on the red planet.

During the missions, players face situations that simulate the difficulties of a possible settlement on Mars, such as shortages of water, oxygen, food and energy. Through these experiences, they develop critical thinking, learn to manage resources and understand the consequences of their choices.

Beyond encouraging space exploration, the game seeks to make children aware that Mars is not a perfect alternative for humanity. Even with technological progress, no other planet offers Earth's natural conditions. Our mission is to show that exploring the universe is important, but preserving our home is essential!
story: Year: 2045. Earth faces climate change, environmental degradation and resource shortages.
NASA creates Project New Horizon to study a future human presence on other planets.
The destination is Mars. Four astronauts leave for a 10-day experimental expedition.
After landing, communication with Earth fails. Supplies and equipment must be reassessed.
The support team arrives only on Day 10. Until then, resources must be preserved and everyone kept safe.
You will take part through a NASA simulation. Choose your astronaut!

days.title: Dust storm
days.situation: A huge dust storm covers the sky. Weak sunlight reaches the solar panels, and we need to save energy.
days.science: Mars has dust storms that reduce sunlight for solar panels, and dust builds up on equipment.

choices.label: A — Turn off non-essential equipment
choices.why: Saving energy keeps important systems running, but switching off comfort and leisure increases stress.

choices.label: B — Keep all equipment running
choices.why: Lighting and comfort support well-being, but batteries run out faster.

choices.label: C — Go outside to clean the solar panels
choices.why: Clean panels capture more light, but going out in the storm exposes the team to risks.

days.title: Radiation alert
days.situation: Sensors warn that the team could receive a higher radiation dose. How can we protect ourselves without using all our resources?
days.science: Mars has a thin atmosphere and no strong global magnetic field. Its surface provides little protection from energetic particles from the Sun.

choices.label: A — Reinforce the shelter with available materials
choices.why: Shielding reduces additional exposure, but does not erase radiation already received.

choices.label: B — Continue outdoor activities
choices.why: Outdoor tasks are completed, but the team is much more exposed.

choices.label: C — Suspend outdoor activities and stay in the habitat
choices.why: Staying protected allows rest, but uses food while we wait.

days.title: Oxygen production failure
days.situation: The equipment that produces oxygen from gas in the Martian atmosphere has failed.
days.science: The Martian atmosphere is mostly CO₂. NASA’s MOXIE experiment showed that CO₂ can be turned into oxygen.

choices.label: A — Use some of the oxygen reserve
choices.why: The reserve keeps the air breathable while the team organizes, but reduces supplies.

choices.label: B — Try to repair the production machine
choices.why: If the repair works, we recover oxygen, but fixing it takes a lot of energy.

choices.label: C — Turn off secondary equipment and prioritize oxygen
choices.why: Prioritizing life support helps, but discomfort affects the team.

days.title: Critical water level
days.situation: Our water supply is falling. We need water to drink, cook and maintain hygiene.
days.science: There is water ice on Mars, mainly at the poles and below ground. Water is also recycled on missions.

choices.label: A — Ration water immediately
choices.why: Rationing makes supplies last longer, but drinking less harms health.

choices.label: B — Repair the recycling system
choices.why: Recovering used water increases supplies, but the system consumes energy.

choices.label: C — Send a small team to look for ice
choices.why: Finding ice helps, but the trip uses energy and involves risks.

days.title: Silence from Earth
days.situation: We sent a message asking for guidance, but the reply is taking a long time.
days.science: Radio signals take about 3 to 22 minutes to travel from Mars to Earth. NASA uses the Deep Space Network to communicate with distant missions.

choices.label: A — Follow emergency protocols
choices.why: Procedures prepared in advance prevent improvisation and provide safety.

choices.label: B — Wait for Earth’s reply before acting
choices.why: Waiting seems safer, but idle time consumes resources.

choices.label: C — Use backup communication equipment
choices.why: The equipment may restore contact and reassure the team, but uses energy.

days.title: Carbon dioxide buildup
days.situation: A sensor shows that carbon dioxide (the gas we breathe out) is rising inside the habitat.
days.science: In space habitats, CO₂ must be continuously removed from the air by life-support systems.

choices.label: A — Activate the backup filter
choices.why: The backup filter removes CO₂ from the air and protects the team, but uses energy.

choices.label: B — Turn off secondary equipment and prioritize filters
choices.why: Reducing consumption keeps essential filters running.

choices.label: C — Stay in the affected compartment
choices.why: This saves energy, but breathing air with too much CO₂ harms health.

days.title: Food supplies are shrinking
days.situation: Food must last until the end of the mission. How should we organize meals?
days.science: NASA studies long-lasting food and even growing plants in space for long missions.

choices.label: A — Organize meals and control portions
choices.why: Planning portions reduces waste and keeps the team fed.

choices.label: B — Eat a full meal to recover energy
choices.why: A nutritious meal helps well-being, but greatly reduces food supplies.

choices.label: C — Save the most nutritious food
choices.why: Saving food helps in an emergency, but eating less now weakens the team.

days.title: The habitat is too cold
days.situation: The temperature inside the habitat is dropping. We need to keep the team warm.
days.science: Mars has an average temperature of about −60 °C. It can get even colder at night.

choices.label: A — Increase habitat heating
choices.why: A suitable temperature protects health, but heating takes a lot of energy.

choices.label: B — Turn off secondary equipment and keep heating on
choices.why: Saving energy on other equipment allows essential heating.

choices.label: C — Wear thermal clothing and reduce heating a little
choices.why: Clothing helps conserve heat, but the team feels colder.

days.title: Habitat leak
days.situation: An alarm indicates a loss of pressure in part of the habitat.
days.science: Air pressure on Mars is less than 1% of Earth’s pressure. The habitat must stay well sealed.

choices.label: A — Isolate the leaking compartment
choices.why: Closing passages stops air loss from affecting the entire habitat.

choices.label: B — Repair the seal directly
choices.why: A successful repair reduces air loss, but is tiring and risky.

choices.label: C — Move the team to another compartment
choices.why: Moving away from the damaged area protects people, but air keeps escaping.

days.title: The final great storm
days.situation: Another dust storm threatens our energy on the very day the support team arrives!
days.science: Dust storms can cover the whole planet and last for weeks.

choices.label: A — Activate maximum energy-saving mode
choices.why: Turning off non-essential equipment conserves energy, but causes discomfort.

choices.label: B — Use the emergency batteries
choices.why: Batteries provide heating and comfort, but exhaust the reserve.

choices.label: C — Prioritize life support and reduce other systems
choices.why: Directing resources to keep the team alive is balanced, but uses food.

emergencies.title: Pressure loss during the night
emergencies.situation: A small piece of space material hit the habitat and damaged a seal. Air is slowly escaping!

choices.label: A — Immediately isolate the damaged compartment
choices.why: This protects people, but some air is lost and systems work to keep the area isolated.

choices.label: B — Repair the seal from inside
choices.why: The emergency repair controls the leak, but requires energy and is tiring.

choices.label: C — Put on spacesuits and repair from outside
choices.why: This may solve it quickly, but going outside at night in an emergency is very risky.

emergencies.title: Fire in the energy compartment
emergencies.situation: A smoke alarm wakes the team! An electrical fault has started a fire in the battery compartment.

choices.label: A — Turn off power to the compartment and isolate it
choices.why: A safe decision, but an important part of the energy supply becomes unavailable.

choices.label: B — Activate the fire suppression system
choices.why: This fights the fire and protects the team, but consumes energy and affects the air.

choices.label: C — Try to save the batteries
choices.why: This may recover energy, but smoke and fire put everyone in great danger.

emergencies.title: Contaminated water
emergencies.situation: A sensor detected a contaminant in the water recycling system. Nobody can drink this water!

choices.label: A — Immediately turn off the recycling system
choices.why: This protects health, but leaves less water until repairs.

choices.label: B — Activate the backup filtration system
choices.why: This recovers safe water, but needs a lot of energy.

choices.label: C — Improvise a filter with available materials
choices.why: This temporary solution is unreliable: untested water must not be considered safe to drink.

andreas.name: Andreas
andreas.quote: In space, knowledge is as important as oxygen. We need to think before acting!

laika.name: Laika
laika.quote: The universe is full of questions waiting to be answered. Shall we discover some together?

lina.name: Lina
lina.quote: A great mission is only possible when we look after one another!

tasks.name: Reconnect electrical circuits
tasks.instructions: Three wires (red, blue, yellow) on the left and three shuffled connectors on the right. Connect each wire to the connector of the same color; if you make a mistake, try again.
tasks.fact: NASA’s Spirit and Opportunity rovers used solar panels. Martian dust reduced the energy they could capture.

tasks.name: Restart the oxygen generator
tasks.instructions: A panel with a 4-digit code and a clue (e.g. “the last digit is twice the first”). A wrong answer resets the panel with a new clue.
tasks.fact: MOXIE, carried by the Perseverance rover, demonstrated that oxygen can be produced from Martian CO₂.

tasks.name: Align the communication antenna
tasks.instructions: Two controls (horizontal and vertical). A meter shows signal strength; reaching green (>92%) completes the task.
tasks.fact: NASA uses the Deep Space Network, a network of large antennas around Earth, to communicate with missions on Mars.

tasks.name: Clean the solar panels
tasks.instructions: A panel with 64 dusty sectors (some need 2 passes). Clean 90% in 50 seconds. Wind gusts make clean sectors dusty again.
tasks.fact: Spirit and Opportunity depended on solar energy; dust and the atmosphere reduced the energy available.

tasks.name: Collect a rock sample
tasks.instructions: A 7×7 grid with a robotic arm controlled by arrows. Forbidden areas send the arm back to the start. Drill over the rock and store it in the tube.
tasks.fact: Perseverance’s robotic arm is about 2.1 meters long and studies rocks and collects samples on Mars.

tasks.name: Organize water filtration
tasks.instructions: Four shuffled modules. Select in order: Water intake → Filtration → Quality check → Reservoir.
tasks.fact: NASA develops life-support systems that recover, monitor, treat and store water for long missions.

tasks.name: Plot a safe rover route
tasks.instructions: A 6×6 grid map. Plot a route one square at a time from A to B, avoiding craters, within 60 seconds.
tasks.fact: Martian rovers use cameras and autonomous navigation to identify obstacles and avoid dangerous terrain.

tasks.name: Check the spacesuit
tasks.instructions: Match four components (oxygen, ventilation, CO₂ removal, communication) to their functions; then press TEST.
tasks.fact: A spacesuit supplies oxygen, removes exhaled CO₂, circulates air, provides electricity and enables communication.

tasks.name: Catalog and store samples
tasks.instructions: Place three tubes with similar codes (MRS-0418, MRS-0481, MRS-4018) in the correct compartment according to the table.
tasks.fact: Perseverance stores samples in sealed tubes and can leave them on the surface for a future mission to retrieve.

sources.title: NASA — MOXIE completes its Mars mission
NASA — Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS)
NASA — 7 Things to Know About Space Communications

oxygen.text: Our bodies need oxygen to function. The atmosphere of Mars is mostly carbon dioxide, so we cannot breathe it. Without reserves and systems supplying breathable air, the team must stop the mission.

water.text: The team needs water to drink and prepare food. Used water is recovered and treated at the base. When supplies run out, this cycle cannot meet the team’s needs and the mission must stop.

food.text: Astronauts need food to meet their nutritional needs during a mission. Without food reserves, the team cannot continue safely. In this simulation, food reaching zero interrupts the mission.

energy.text: The base needs electricity to operate its equipment and life-support systems. Dust storms on Mars can reduce the sunlight available to solar panels. In this simulation, energy reaching zero means the base can no longer support a safe mission.

radiation.text: Mars has a thin atmosphere and no strong global magnetic field, leaving the team exposed to energetic particles. Radiation exposure can endanger astronauts’ health. In this simulation, 100% radiation is the safety limit that interrupts the mission, not a real-world dose measurement.

health.text: Surviving in space requires several kinds of care at once: breathable air, safe water, food and temperature control. When these systems stop protecting the team, health is at risk. In the game, zero health represents this limit.
